en: (Bagalāmukhīpañcāṅga) (Extent: 153 folios, Saṃvat 1939)
(Subject:
Tantra) Oṃ. Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Homage to the illustrious Balāmukhī. Homage to the illustrious Īśvara.
The Lord of the Gods of gods said: "I shall speak the most excellent among secrets, the supreme chapter of Vagalāmukhī, which is to be kept hidden."
This Vidyā, worshipped by the gods,
which possesses the power of the foremost goddesses,
must not be given to just anyone in the Kali age.
Rare in the three worlds, one should perform the morning duties and then carry out the worship of the Cakra;
having performed the worship, one should recite the mantra.
Tārā, who bestows the fruits of the fourfold aims of life, Tottalā, Śyāmā, Tāriṇī, Camanomanā, Vaindavī, and Vaiśībhā.
The practitioner of the mantra of Bagalāmukhī, whose deity is Gaurī,
bestows the eight siddhis wherever he may reside; there is no doubt of this.
Where Śakra is not present, disease does not prevail there;
therefore, this Śrīvidyā Bagalāmukhī must be kept secret.
At night, the practitioners should recite its mantra according to their ability; at midday,
O Lord of Gods, that deity becomes submissive.
Therefore, O Maheśānī, out of devotion for you who are difficult to reach, I shall today speak of the extraction of the yantra; O Gopī, keep this extraction of the yantra secret.
Having first extracted the *praṇava* as the womb (*yoni*),
the practitioner should thereafter join it with the ether (*viyat*), earth (*bhūmi*), fire (*ratī*), and the bindu.

Next, one should know the supreme mantra with two heads (the *dviśiras*) ending in the syllable *Indu* (the Moon); from that, one should extract the *pallava* (sprout), which is "Vagalamukhi" (*vaid-*) in the Veda.
May [the mantra] paralyze the speech of all evil-faced ones, having given the tongue as a stake,
and may it surely destroy their intellect.
With *mṛtsnā* as the seed-syllable and *tāra* at the end, one should place two *piṭhas*; this is remembered as the excellent mantra. [It consists of] forty [syllables].
This mantra of five syllables bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Goddess, I shall now explain its supreme manifestation in due order— listen.
It should be kept secret from the wicked and from those who harbor hatred; likewise, it is revealed: Oṃ hlīṃ bagalāmukhi sarvaduṣṭamu...
Paralyze his speech, paralyze it! Nail down his tongue! Destroy his intellect! Hlīṃ oṃ svāhā. (25)
O Goddess of the lords of the Asuras, there is never any fault in this nyāsa; there is no obstacle, nor is there such conduct, nor is there any such reversal.
This Bhagalamantra, which is the very embodiment of nectar and is exceedingly difficult to obtain, is manifest before you.
O Maheśānī,
the procedure for the ritual service (puraścaryā) of one hundred thousand repetitions is prescribed; by the mere recollection of this, the sin of ten million killings is destroyed.

I shall now describe her meditation, which is to be kept secret from men in the Kali age. As for the meditation: she possesses the luster of a thousand rising suns and wears a garland of severed heads.
Adorned, wearing yellow garments,
fond of yellow, decorated with yellow garlands, seated upon a yellow throne, and radiant.
She whose face displays a laugh that has transcended the ghora and ahāsita [smiles],
who holds a mace, a sword, and a tongue in her hands, and who bears a mallet as a weapon, [drinking] the essence of human skulls...
Her face resembled molten gold, her hair was tawny, she was made of clay,
devoted to drinking honey-wine, and possessed various [ornaments].
"I remember Vagalāmukhī, adorned with battle-ornaments"— thus has the meditation been proclaimed by me, which is difficult to find in the three worlds.
I shall now describe the extraction of the yantra, which is to be kept secret in the Kali age on this earth. First,
having drawn a hexagon, draw an upward-pointing [triangle] above it.
Furthermore, O Sovereign of the Gods, one should contract the triangle in the middle, below the yantra; indeed,
one should move within the triangle in the center of the triangle.
One should draw an eight-cornered yantra marked with three circular lines; outside,
it is said to have four petals, surrounded by a circle.
Furthermore, outside of that, the best of practitioners should draw three lines and a four-gated enclosure for the Lord of the Yantra,
Vagalamukhi, and the enemy.
This which causes immobilization must not be given; O Mistress, it should be guarded with great effort. Furthermore, for the purpose of subjugation, one should write it on gold.
One should write it on copper for the purpose of delusion, on lead for the purpose of immobilization, on iron for the purpose of killing, and on tin for the purpose of eradication.
The practitioner should keep this supreme yantra,
endowed with power, hidden in the Kali age; having quickly divided the root mantra within the yantra, he should [employ it].
One should worship the twenty deities of trade. A man should place the syllable *TĀRAṂ* above; below that is the syllable *MṚTTIKĀ*;
and below that, the syllable *NARA*.
One should place the seed-syllable of Śiva below that;
below that, the seed-syllable of Tamas; below that, the excellent seed-syllable is remembered; [and finally] the seed-syllable of Śūnya.
Below that, further down, the best of practitioners should write the syllable *amṛta* (am) and two crescent moons (*uṇḍu*) in the center of the yantra.
O Pārvatī, listen to the names of the goddesses in truth: Totalā,
Tāriṇī, Tārā, Śītalā, and Camanī.
Manā, Vaikharī, Khecarī, Śyāmā, Navamī, and Vagalāmukhī—
these six should always be worshipped by practitioners for their welfare.
One who desires [fulfillment] should worship the Goddess Vagalāmukhī with mantras in the three triangles; having thus worshipped her with these mantras, the yantra is always [efficacious].
O Mistress of the Heart, these four should be worshipped by the best of practitioners on the outer petals;
outside of that, on the eight petals.
And the deities to be worshipped are Bālā,
Bhargaśikhā, Durgā, Bhavānī,
Bhadrakālī, and Mahālakṣmī.
One should worship Māyādevatā, Vaindaveśvarī,
and these [deities] on the eight petals; one should then worship the gatekeepers,
beginning with Gaṇeśa and Varuṇa.
One should worship the illustrious Dharmarāja,
as well as Indra,
the gods, the guardians of the directions, and the door-keepers.
This, proclaimed as the most excellent secret, must not be given to just anyone.
I shall now describe the rites of paralyzing, killing, deluding, attracting, and subjugating.
I shall now describe *kāra*, *uccāṭana*, and *vidveṣa*; whatever the specific desire may be, such is the ritual action to be performed.
The practitioner, having risen at sunrise, should perform the libation:
*oṃ hlīṃ gaṃ gaṇeśaṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ*; *oṃ hlīṃ voṃ varuṇaṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ*; *oṃ hlīṃ*.
Śrīṃ Śrīṃ, I offer libations to the Ten Vidyās; obeisance. Oṃ Hlīṃ Trīṃ, I offer libations to Dharmarāja; obeisance. Oṃ, I offer libations to Vagalāmukhī and her retinue; obeisance.

"Namaḥ hlīṃ oṃ svāhā tarpayāmi namaḥ" (3). Having thus offered libations according to the rule, one should sip water three times for purification and perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Likewise, O Goddess of Gods, one causes the enemy's semen to become immobilized with haridrā by means of the root mantra; and likewise with blue flowers and fish.

One should perform a fire sacrifice with substances for killing according to the prescribed rite; by means of black substances, the enemy shall go the way of death, while milk, ghee, and curd [bring about] prosperity.
With incense and jasmine flowers, one should likewise perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the root mantra; thus, one will certainly delude the three worlds. [The mantra is: *vukamāṃ*.
The practitioner, being well-restrained, should perform the fire sacrifice with these [substances] mixed with ghee and cow’s urine; certainly, attraction will occur. Guḍa...
The practitioner should perform the fire-oblation with flowers mixed with ghee and milk, and with the blood of a menstruating woman and of one who is not female.
All the deities beginning with Brahmā,
the hosts of Apsarases beginning with Rambhā, and the guardians of the quarters beginning with Indra, were brought under his control.
Immediately after that, one should perform a homa with salt, oil, ghee, and milk-rice mixed with the excrement of a cat.
By reciting the root mantra of one's own [deity] over clay from a well mixed with ghee,
hair from a woman, and the flesh of a goat, the eradication of the sun, fire, and enemies shall occur.

The best of practitioners should likewise offer oblations of fish-ears and breast-milk; by this act, performed through body, mind, and speech, there shall be the inciting of hatred against the enemy. [This is done] with sheep's milk.
The practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice with human flesh, hair from the pubic region, and clarified butter; he will obtain the son of a barren woman.
Likewise, with curd and buttermilk, [he will obtain] a cow.
By performing the homa with milk and ghee, the practitioner shall immediately become a treasury of knowledge;
such is the nature of the practitioner's own desire.
One should perform such a homa and shall obtain all desires; by performing a homa with cotton,
a king shall become submissive immediately.
This chapter, however, is to be kept secret; it has been revealed out of devotion for you. It is unmanifest, the supreme secret, and should not be given to just anyone who seeks worldly enjoyment.
It bestows [all] desires, yet it must be hidden and kept secret like a noble womb.
Thus ends the chapter on Śrī Vagalāmukhī in the venerable Īśvara Tantra.
Now the ritual manual for worship (*pūjā-paddhati*) is set forth.
The venerable Goddess said: "Oṃ! O Śrīkaṇṭha, ocean of compassion, you who bring life to the world, [this is] the manual..."
"You ought to speak regarding the worship of the chief goddess Tiṃvagalā.
Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall speak—removing all impurities through devotion to you."
Make this hymn of praise to Vagalāmukhī, who is more secret than the most secret,
a bestower of desired fruits for men, gods,
and even for me; whoever performs its worship...
For one who has been consecrated by this mantra, success is not far off. Then, the practitioner, rising from his seat and going near water, should quickly drink it.
The mantra for the three purifications is: Oṃ hrīṃ vidyā-tattvāya svāhā, śrīṃ guru-tattvāya svāhā, klīṃ devī-tattvāya svāhā. i.
Having sipped water (ācamana), one should go a distance away and perform the evacuation of waste; having discarded feces, urine, and so forth,
a person should perform the rite of purification while reciting the *praṇava* mantra.
Having joyfully performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma)— namely, inhalation (pūraka) for sixteen [counts], retention (kuṃbhaka) for sixty-four, and exhalation (recaka) for thirty-two—
one should perform the ritual of breath-restraint while cleaning the teeth.
Having purified his teeth with the seed-syllable *svāhā*, the best of practitioners, the mantra-master, should fetch clay and divide it into three portions. (4)
The practitioner should purify the clay with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the seed-syllable of Amṛtā;
he should remove the garments from his limbs with the root-mantra (*mūla*) and purify the clay.
One should perform the invocation of the sacred fords (tīrthāvāhana) according to the prescribed ritual:
"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī— be present in these waters!"

The best of practitioners, having thus consecrated the clay with the root mantra, should not cast it upon the ground; rather, he should duly invoke the sacred waters (tīrtha) and perform the rite of invocation.
O Bagalāmukhī, adorned with excellent ornaments, holding a mace in your hand and seated upon a corpse,
come respectfully to this water accompanied by the syllable *hlīṃ*.
Then, the best of practitioners should collect clay from within the water;
the mantrin should quickly smear that clay upon his own limbs with the root mantra. Thereafter, he should... [praṇamya]... the Lord.
One should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) while meditating on the sun;
[one should worship] with "Oṃ hsauṃḥ," to the one whose vehicle is the seven horses, and to the Lord of Lords, Ravi, homage to You!

One should perform *prāṇāyāma* for the one whose eyes are the moon and the drop (*bindu*)— [specifically] filling (*pūraka*) for sixty-four [breaths], retaining (*kumbhaka*) for thirty-two, and exhaling (*recaka*) for sixteen.
Then, three sips of water (*ācamana*), with the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ śivata*.
*Tattvāya svāhā* (1); *Oṃ śrīṃ gurutatvāya svāhā* (2); *Oṃ klīṃ śaktitatvāya svāhā* (3). Having sipped water (*ācamya*) with these, one should meditate upon the Guru: *Oṃ*.
Having meditated thus: "I bow to the supreme Guru, who is the form that destroys the darkness and gloom of ignorance, a treasury of compassion, and purified by the ocean of the scriptures."

One should regard the Guru as a deity; having descended into the water, the practitioner, the best among the virtuous, should first perform the unsurpassed bath and purify himself with the Gāyatrī mantra.
A practitioner of mantras should wash his face three times with the root mantra and the seed-syllable *svāhā*;
thereafter, he should perform the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandhana*) with the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).
With devotion, one should quickly offer three handfuls of water to the Sun with the Mūla-mantra; then, having sipped water (ācamana), one should recite one's own Mūla-mantra three times, O Goddess.

O Maheśāni, one who is not yet a perfected practitioner (asādhaka) should bathe in water or [use] wood; there he should wear a loincloth (kaupīna) and perform the ritual of the junctions of time (saṃdhyā-vidhi). There, first of all, the Bhā...

The mantra-expert should offer the *ārāya* [oblation] with the mantra, as well as the *argha* and the *añjali* of water, and perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Oṃ hsauṃḥ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ sū.

Oṃ, obeisance with joined palms to Sūryā who desires the guest-offering. (3) Oṃ hrāṃ hrauṃ hraiṃ hsauḥ, obeisance with joined palms to Sūryā. (3) Then one should bow to her who resembles the *japā* flower.
"I bow to that Sun of great splendor, the destroyer of darkness and the remover of all sins.
Then, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Then one should mutter the Gāyatrī: *oṃ hlauṃ brahmāstravidyāyai vidmahe oṃ hluṃ pītāmbarāyai śatrustambhinyai dhīmahi oṃ hlīṃ*.

Having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity with this *gāyatrī* mantra: "O Bagalāmukhī, O Ghorā, impel this for us," one should meditate upon the Goddess, [offering] to the gurus...
Having performed the recitation of the *saṃkalpa* with the words "I offer," and having meditated upon the Goddess there— appearing like the sixteenth digit of the moon,
clad in yellow garments, and adorned with ornaments—
She wears matted locks as yellow as a calf's tail, is served by hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā,
and holds the life-force and the armlets of the enemy within the chest of that foe.
One should meditate upon the supreme goddess Haṃbagalāmukhī, who is the immobilizer and is currently dawn-red;
having thus meditated, one should recite the root mantra according to one's ability.
A practitioner desiring success should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) ten times the number of recitations (japa). Having sipped water (ācamana) there with the root mantra,
the practitioner should then recite the root mantra.
The best of practitioners should recite the armor-stotra (kavaca) and the thousand names;
then, the knower of mantras should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with the root mantra. Then, the libation...
Namaḥ oṃ hlīṃ, I satiate the Guru who bestows the weapon-vidyā; namaḥ. (1) Oṃ hlāṃ, I satiate the Supreme Guru of the vidyās beginning with the paralyzing [spell]; namaḥ.
Oṃ hlaḥ, I offer libation to the Guru, the bestower of the root-vidyā; obeisance. (3) Oṃ hlīṃ, I offer libation to the Guru Brahmānandanātha; obeisance. (1) Oṃ hlāṃ, Viśvakse...
Oṃ hlāṃ, I satiate the Guru Ānandanātha; obeisance. (3) Oṃ hlaḥ, I satiate the Guru Śivānandanātha; obeisance. (3) Oṃ hlīṃ kraṃ, I satiate Uttarā.
Namaḥ oṃ hlīṃ strīṃ tāriṇīṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ (2). Oṃ hluṃ tārāṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ (2).
Oṃ śrīṃ śītalāṃ tarpayāmi namaḥ.
Namaḥ reṃ prīṃ, I satisfy Manonmanā, namaḥ. Oṃ hlīṃ vīṃ, I satisfy Vaikharī, namaḥ.
Reṃ khrīṃ, I satisfy Khecarī, namaḥ. Reṃ krīṃ Śyāmā...
I satiate Māṃ; obeisance! Reṃ Hlīṃ Svāhā;
I satiate Bagalāmukhī; obeisance! (9) I satiate the father, the giver of life; Oṃ; obeisance!
Hlīṃ, I satiate the grandfather; obeisance. Reṃ Oṃ Reṃ Hlīṃ, I satiate the great-grandfather; obeisance. Oṃ Hlīṃ, I satiate the great-great-grandfather; obeisance.
Oṃ hlīṃ, I offer libations to my paternal ancestors; obeisance. Oṃ hlīṃ, I offer libations to my maternal ancestors; obeisance. Reṃ, I offer libations to my maternal grandfather; obeisance. Reṃ.

I offer libations to the paternal great-grandfather; obeisance. Reṃ, I offer libations to the elder paternal great-grandfather; obeisance. Reṃ Reṃ, I offer libations to the paternal grandfather born of [this] lineage; obeisance.
Reṃ Aiṃ Sauḥ, I offer libations to Sarasvatī; obeisance. Reṃ Aiṃ Sauḥ, I offer libations to Sumukhī; obeisance. Reṃ Hlīṃ Sauḥ, I offer libations to Bālā; obeisance. Oṃ Hlīṃ.
Hsauḥ, I offer libation to Bhargaśikhā; obeisance. Oṃ hlīṃ hsauṃḥ, I offer libation to Bhairavī; obeisance.
Oṃ cchrīṃ, I offer libation to Chinnamastikā.
Maḥ reṃ, I offer libations to Durgā, obeisance. Oṃ hlīṃ hrīṃ, I offer libations to Bhavānī, obeisance. Reṃ krīṃ bhaiṃ, I offer libations to Bhadrakālī, obeisance. Oṃ hlīṃ.
Klīṃ, obeisance, I satiate the Blessed Lady; Reṃ Śrīṃ, obeisance, I satiate Mahāmāyā; Bhaiṃ Vaiṃ, obeisance, I satiate Dhaveśvarī.
Oṃ hlīṃ gaṃ, I satiate Gaṇeśa; obeisance. Oṃ hlīṃ voṃ, I satiate Varuṇa; obeisance. Oṃ hlīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ, I satiate the Ten Vidyās; obeisance.
Oṃ hlīṃ trīṃ, I satiate Dharmarāja; obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate Vagalāmukhī together with her retinue; obeisance. Hlīṃ oṃ svāhā, I satiate [her]; obeisance.
Having thus satisfied [the deity] according to the rules and having drunk three mouthfuls of water for sipping, and having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma),
one should bow to the Lord Bhāskara; having bowed, [one continues].

"Having worshipped Bhāskara with devotion, one should return home"; having thus performed [the rite] without effort, the practitioner should return to his own house and commence the worship of the door (*dvārapūjā*).
Oṃ hrīṃ dvāṃ, obeisance to Dvāraśrī; oṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Dehalī; oṃ, obeisance to Aliṃdā; oṃ hrīṃ lāṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī; oṃ vroṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī; oṃ.
*Mrīṃ* to Māhendrī, *namaḥ*; *Oṃ Śrīṃ* to Śāṅkarī, *namaḥ*; in the center, *klīṃ hlīṃ* to Bagalāmukhī, *namaḥ*. Having thus completed the worship of the doors, [perform] *prāṇāyāma*.

Having performed three *prāṇāyāmas*, the practitioner should perform the immediate purification of the seat (*viṣṭara-śodhana*) with his own root-mantra and his own mantra; thus the mantrin should proceed. *Oṃ a...*

Of this mantra for purifying the seat of Śrī, Merupṛṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is the meter (chandaḥ), Kūrma is the deity (devatā), Śeṣa is the seed-syllable (bīja), and the directional elephants (dig-nāgāḥ) are the power (śakti).
*Śakti*, *Dharaṇīpati*, and *Kīlaka*.
The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purification of the seat (*āsana-śodhana*). *Oṃ hlīṃ prīṃ namaḥ to the ghost-seat (pretāsana)*. *Oṃ hrāṃ śrīṃ*.
Oṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva in the form of Śiva;
Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to the one seated upon the thousand-petaled lotus throne;
Oṃ hrīṃ, [salutation] to the jeweled pavilion and its altar.
Having purified the seat with "Nāyanamaḥ oṃ hlīṃ prīṃ devīvāhanāya mahākālāya namaḥ phaṭ svāhā," one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The wise one should worship Suśikhā and Gāyatrī with their own root-mantras; having worshipped them with Gāyatrī,
he should sip water three times and recite the root-mantra as much as possible.
O Maheśānī, having performed the nyāsa and other rites, and having meditated upon the Goddess Vagalāmukhī in that manner, one should worship her.
Oṃ. Of this Śrī Brahmāstra-vidyā, the Śrī...
For the mantra of Vagalāmukhī: Brahmā is the ṛṣi, Uṣṇik is the meter, Śrī-Vagalāmukhī is the deity,
Hṛllīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Oṃ is the power (śakti), and Svāhā is the pin (kīla).
In this regard, the injunction for the recitation (*japa*) of the *Śrī-caturvidha-puruṣārtha-mantra* is as follows: *Oṃ atha mūlam | Oṃ hlīṃ bagalāmukhi sarva-duṣṭa-vācaṃ mukhaṃ padaṃ staṃ*.
*Bhayastaṃbhaya jihvāṃ kīlaya (2) buddhiṃ vināśaya (2) hlīṃ oṃ svāhā*. This is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Now, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *Oṃ*, salutation to Brahmā, the seer (*ṛṣi*), upon the head (*śiras*).
*Ra* is for the *uṣṇik* meter, salutation to the face; *va* is for the goddess Galāmukhī, salutation to the heart;
*hlīṃ* is for the seed-syllable, salutation to the secret place; *oṃ* is for the power (*śakti*).
*Namaḥ* to the feet; *svāhā* to the *kīlaka*; *namaḥ* to the navel; *namaḥ* to all limbs; *oṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ* to the head; *oṃ gurutatvāya namaḥ* to the mouth.
Oṃ *khe* śaktitattvāya namaḥ to the heart; oṃ *brahmāstra-vidyātattvāya* namaḥ to the navel;
oṃ *śivaśaktitattvāya* namaḥ to all limbs.
Thus ends the Nyāsa of the Tattvas. Now begins the Mātṛkā Nyāsa: Oṃ Aṃ Āṃ Iṃ Īṃ Hlāṃ, salutation to the head;
Uṃ Ūṃ Ṛṃ Ṝṃ Hlīṃ, salutation to the mouth; Ḷṃ Ḹṃ... [and so forth].
*Eṃ eṃ hluṃ namaḥ* at the navel; *Oṃ oṃ auṃ aṃ aṃḥ hlaḥ namaḥ* on all limbs; *Kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ yaṃ hlāṃ namaḥ* on the head;
*Caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ hlīṃ namaḥ* on the mouth.
Ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ laṃ hlūṃ namaḥ to the heart;
taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ vaṃ hlaiṃ namaḥ to the navel; paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ hlauṃḥ namaḥ to the feet.
*Śaṃ saṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ hlaḥ namaḥ* on all the limbs—thus is the *varṇanyāsa*. Now, the *mūlamantranyāsa*:
*hlāṃ* *namaḥ* to both thumbs; *hlīṃ* *namaḥ* to both index fingers.
*Maḥ* to the middle fingers; *Hlaiṃ* to the ring fingers; *Hlauṃ* to the little fingers; *Hlaḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands.
Now, the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*): *hlāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hlīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*;
*hluṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ*; *hlaiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*; *hlauṃ* to the three eyes.
Having performed the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra *yaivaṣaṭ hlaḥ astrāya phaṭ*, the practitioner should meditate upon the Goddess in the center of the Svadhā-vault,
upon a jeweled pavilion and a precious altar, seated upon a lion.
I remember the Goddess seated upon a lion-throne, her complexion deep yellow,
her limbs adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and garlands,
holding a mallet and the tongue of an enemy.

Having meditated thus, the practitioner who seeks to accomplish the mantra should perform the recitation (*japa*). Having performed the recitation according to his capacity, he should then commence the worship (*pūjā*). Now follows the procedure for worship (*pūjā-paddhati*).
O Sovereign Goddess, the practitioner of mantra should first worship the gatekeepers; then, having worshipped the eight goddesses, the adept should worship the four [inner goddesses];
then, having worshipped the eight goddesses [again].
The practitioner, the seeker of mantras, having performed the recitation (*japa*) according to his ability,
should commence the worship of the yantra; the mantra-knower should worship Navamī-Bagā in the center of the yantra.
Now, the worship of the door-keepers (*dvārapāla-pūjā*) for the face-to-face (*lāmukhī*) [practice]:
the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "Oṃ glūṃ, I worship Gaṇeśa; obeisance. Then: "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ glauṃ, [I worship] Gaṇeśa."
*Oṃ yaguṃūṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*—thus in the east. *Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ vīṃ varuṇāya kuṃṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*—thus in the west. *Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīdāya*.
"KṚĪṂ KUVERĀYAKRŪṂ ṬHAḤ ṬHAḤ ṬHAḤ SVĀHĀ"—thus in the north.
"OṂ ŚRĪṂ HRĪṂ KLĪṂ DRĪṂ DHARMARĀJĀYAKRŪṂ ṬHAḤ ṬHAḤ ṬHAḤ SVĀHĀ"—thus in the south. These are the door-keepers.
Now follows the eight-petaled lotus worship (aṣṭadalapūjā).
Oṃ vālāṃ pūjayāmi namaḥ; aiṃ klīṃ sauṃḥ vālāyai namaḥ—thus in the east. Oṃ sauṃḥ bhargaśikhāyai namaḥ—thus in the southeast. Oṃ śrīṃ...
"Hrīṃ duṃ, obeisance to Durgā"—thus [on] the south. "Oṃ oṃ hrīṃ oṃ śrīṃ aiṃ sauṃḥ, obeisance to Bhavānī"—thus on the Nṛti-petal.
"Krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hruṃ hruṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ bhaiṃ."
*Bhadrakālibhaiṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hruṃ hruṃ krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ svāhā bhadrakālyai namaḥ*— thus in the west;
*oṃ hroṃ bhaiṃ bhagavāsāyai namaḥ*— thus in the north.
In the north-east corner: "Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ mahāmāyāyai namaḥ"; thus in the north: "Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ sauḥ vaiṃ daveśvaryai namaḥ"; and likewise in the north-east.
Having fully worshipped the six goddesses, one should worship the four goddesses:
"Oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ sauṃḥ, obeisance to Sarasvatī"—thus in the east; "Aiṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Sumukhī"—thus in the south.
"Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ bhairavyai namaḥ" in the west; "Oṃ śrīṃ aiṃ sauḥ chrīṃ chinnamastikāyai namaḥ" in the north— thus are the four goddesses.

The wise one, the best among mantra-experts, should worship her on the upward-pointing petal joined with the seed-syllable *tāra*; on the previous day, he should worship the goddess Tottalā, the sovereign of the gods, with the mantra: *Oṃ śrīṃ duṃ to*.
*Talāya traitraṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*—thus in the east.
*Oṃ krīṃ hrūṃ sthīṃ tāriṇyai namaḥ*—thus in the southeast. *Oṃ śrīṃ strīṃ kuṃ tārāyai namaḥ*.

In the south: *oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ śītalāyai namaḥ*. In the west (southwest): *oṃ ṣṭraiṃ sauḥ kalīṃ śrīṃ manonmanāyai namaḥ*. In the west: *oṃ aiṃ sauṃḥ klīṃ vīṃ vaikharyai namaḥ*. In the northwest: *oṃ slīṃ khrīṃ*.
"Khecaryai namaḥ" [is] in the north; "krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hruṃ hruṃ" in the south;
"kālike krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ huṃ huṃ svāhā śyāmā bhagavati" [is] in the west.

The practitioner should worship Vagalāmukhī in the northeast with the mantra "tyainamaḥ," located in the middle of the [diagram] petals, adorned with the seed-syllable *svāhā*, and situated above the void (*śūnya*).
Oṃ hlīṃ vagalāyai kṣi sarva-duṣṭa-vāca-mukhaṃ padaṃ staṃbhaya (2) jihvāṃ kīlaya (2) buddhiṃ vināśaya (2) hlīṃ oṃ svāhā baga.

To her who is accompanied by her principal retinue, who possesses weapons and vehicles, *hlīṃ namaḥ*. Likewise, with perfumes, unbroken grains, flowers, and so forth, as well as incense, lamps, and food offerings...
The best of practitioners, having thus worshipped the Goddess with the root mantra along with the five types of offerings,
should worship the vessels.
One should place nine vessels upon a clean cloth with the root mantra of the Nine Goddesses:
*Oṃ hlīṃ Vagalāmukhi hlīṃ oṃ madhupānidrāṃ drīṃ dreṃ draiṃ drauṃ draḥ*.
Having worshipped with "Śukra-śāpa-mocaya-mocaya aiṃ ṭhaḥ klīṃ ṭhaḥ sauṃ ṭhaḥ svāhā," one should offer the vessels and the supreme food offering (naivedya) to the Deity with the root mantra.

The practitioner, for the sake of attaining his own fruit, [should recite]: *Oṃ hlīṃ bagalāmukhi imaṃ baliṃ gṛhṇa (2) hlīṃ oṃ svāhā*. This is the *bali* mantra. Then, [he should offer] flowers to the goddesses.
O Goddess of gods, Mother of the world, adorned with yellow garments and ornaments, may you always grant me success through worship, offerings,
and the recitation of this hymn of praise.
O Goddess Bhuvaneśānī, by means of this thousand names of the King, may you always be pleased; may all practitioners rejoice,
and may [all obstacles] perish.
Vidūṣaka: May this state of Śambhu be mine;
may the Guru be ever gracious to us. I do not know invocation at all, nor do I know worship at all.
"I do not know how to perform the dismissal; may it be forgiven, O Bagalāmukhī.
Thus ends the *Bagalāmukhī Nityapūjā-paddhati* within the *Śrī-Rahasyātira hasya*.
Thus it is concluded; may there be auspiciousness.
(Ṭhīṣ FOḻīO īṣ BḻāṇK) Now the armor (*kavaca*) is being expounded. The venerable Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare to you the secret of the *Svarahasya*."
O Goddess of the Suras, having heard this most secret and well-guarded armor of Bagalāmukhī— which grants all desires in the Kali age and is my supreme and ultimate treasure— please conceal it.
And [he gave] the beautiful armor of Śarajanman (Kārttikeya), named Trailokyavijaya, which is well-guarded, contains mantras within it,
is of the nature of mantra, and is the Vināyaka of perfected vidyās.
O child, know this supreme secret, which is the very embodiment of nectar,
consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, difficult for living beings to attain in the Kali age— complete [and] lacking only one part of five.
"O Lord of Gods, through devotion to you, I have spoken this which is joined with sixty-four syllables consisting of mantras; it must be guarded like a secret womb.
The Goddess said: "O Bhagavān, essence of compassion for the universe..."
Nātha Sureśvara said to Agnibhūti, who was [present] through action, mind, and speech: "Bhairava spoke this armor (*kavaca*) known as *Trailokyavijaya*."
O Pārvatī, for this secret mantra containing the essence, the seer is Devasva Bhairava, the meter is Uṣṇik, the power is Śakti,
and Svāhā is said to be the kīlaka.

The application (viniyoga) has been fully described for this mantra-essence named Śrī Trailokyavijaya, which is dedicated to the worship of Śrī Bagalāmukhī for the attainment of the fruits of the three aims of life (trivarga).
Vacasya Bhairava is the Ṛṣi; Uṣṇik is the Chandas;
Śrīṃ-Bagalāmukhī is the Devatā; Hlīṃ is the Bīja; Oṃ is the Śakti; Svāhā is the Kīlaka; the fruit is the attainment of the three aims of life (Trivarga).
Regarding the application in the ritual practice, Bhairava said: "O Queen of the Gods, one should meditate upon the Goddess and recite the mantra containing the armor (*varma*);
without meditation, there is no accomplishment—this is the truth, so let it be known."
O Pārvatī, now meditate upon her whose hair is illuminated by the moon, who has three eyes, who holds a severed head and a rosary in her hands,
who is youthful, radiant with a yellow garland, reddened by the intoxication of wine, and adorned with a mass of matted locks.
I worship the Blessed One, Vagalāmukhī, whose form is compassion; she who paralyzes enemies, who has a moon-like face, who is resplendent in yellow garments, and who stands upon a corpse.
Thus is the meditation: Oṃ hlīṃ, may the Goddess Vagalāmukhī protect my head; Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ, may the Goddess who causes paralysis protect my forehead; Oṃ aṃ...
May *Īṃ* protect my eyebrows; may *Haṃ* protect my throat, she who removes all affliction; may *Oṃ Haṃ Kṣaṃḥ* protect my eyes, the auspicious Nārasiṃhī; may *Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ* protect my nose.
Ḍauṃ Āṃ Īṃ Bhuvaneśvarī; Oṃ Aiṃ Klīṃ Saḥ may she protect my ears; Iṃ Ūṃ Ūṃ Vaṭeśvarī; Oṃ Krīṃ Huṃ Hrīṃ may she always pervade my nose; Ḍāṃ Ḷṃ Sarasvatī.
Tī oṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ—may she protect my face; oṃ aiṃ Chinnamastikā; oṃ śrīṃ daṃ—may she protect my two ears; oṃ auṃ Dakṣiṇakālikā; oṃ hrīṃ huṃ bhaiṃ.
May Bhadrakālī protect my lower teeth; Oṃ Krīṃ Śrīṃ Śāṃ Rasāṃ, may Śārikā protect my palate, and Khaṃ Gaṃ Ghaṃ.
Oṃ Aiṃ Sauṃḥ, may Mehanu protect my [palate] and Caṃ.
Chaṃ jaṃ manonmanā oṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ mayā pātu jhaṃ ñaṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ Gaṇeśvarī oṃ hrīṃ Skanda u sadā vyāt me ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ caiva Uottalā oṃ hrīṃ.

Śrīṃ, may Mebhujā protect my arms; Taṃ thaṃ daṃ, may Varavarṇinī [protect them]. Oṃ klīṃ sauṃḥ, may Me protect my breasts; dhaṃ naṃ paṃ, may Parameśvarī [protect them]. Oṃ kraṃ kaṃ, may Me protect my chest; phaṃ baṃ...
Oṃ krīṃ kraṃ hrīṃ pātu me kukṣiṃ maṃ yaṃ raṃ Vahnivallabhā; oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ pātu me pārśvaṃ laṃ vaṃ laṃ Vodara-prasūḥ; oṃ hrīṃ.
Huṃ! May Enāmī, the six-faced one, protect my face;
Oṃ Aiṃ Sauḥ! May Saṃhaṃ Hāṭakarūpiṇī protect my back;
Oṃ Klīṃ Aiṃ! May she protect my penis.
Oṃ krīṃ huṃ mekaṭiṃ pātu—
the fifty-syllable Mātṛkā in the form of the slayer of Laṅkā; oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ pātu me guhyaṃ—
oṃ śrīṃ uṃ huṃ sadā may Guhyakeśvarī protect my secret place.
Oṃ juṃ saḥ, may Gaṅgā, who moves through the sky upon a swan, protect my thighs;
Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, may she who is beloved by the hosts of Gaṇas and who removes all sin, protect my shanks. Ṭaṃ ṭāṃ ghaṃ.
Oṃ śrīṃ saḥ:
may Cāmuṇḍā protect my ankles; oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ:
may she who is dear to the world protect my sides; oṃ śrīṃ klīṃ: may she protect [me].
Oṃ auṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ bhaga-udara ā hīṃ me sarvaṃ vapuḥ pātu aṃ aḥ hīṃ Tripureśvarī. Oṃ śrīṃ mayā pūrve sadā vyāptam aṃ āṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ.
Śikhāmukhī—Oṃ Hrīṃ! May she who is ever pervading protect me from the south;
and Tāriṇī—Śrīṃ Hrīṃ!
May Khecarī protect me from the west, [she whose seed-syllables are] Iṃ Taṃ Thaṃ Daṃ. Oṃ.
May *yaṃ* protect me in the north; may *taṃ dhaṃ naṃ paṃ* and *ilaṃ pilā* protect me;
*oṃ śrīṃ māṃ* protect me in the northeast;
*ūṃ phaṃ vaṃ vaiṃ* may *Dhaveśvarī* protect me; *oṃ śrīṃ sauṃḥ* protect me in the southeast.
Yyāṃ ṛṃ bhaṃ maṃ yaṃ, may the Yoginī protect me in the southeast;
oṃ aiṃ māṃ, may [the goddess] always protect me in the southwest; oṃ śrīṃ māṃ, may she protect me in the northwest; ḹṃ laṃ māṃ laṃ, may [she] protect me...
O Keśinī, may you protect me at dawn;
O Tulasī, may Gīśvarī likewise protect me; and at midday, may Śaṅkaravallabhā protect me—Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ, may she protect me!
O Śākambharī, protect me always at dawn; O you who recline upon the ocean, protect me at night; O Hari, protect me at midnight.
Māṃ sāyama aiṃ īṃ śākambharī sadā hrīṃ niśāyāṃ tu māṃ pātu oṃ saṃsāgaraśāyanī klīṃ niśīthe ca māṃ pātu oṃ haṃ hari.
O Hareśvarī, O Klīṃ, O Brāhmī, may this moment pervade me;
O Tripurasundarī, that place which was forgotten and excluded by the armor-mantra— [may it be restored].
Hlīṃ! O Tanaume, protect me from all [sins]! Aṃ Kṣaṃ Hlīṃ!
O Vagalāmukhī! This secret armor (kavaca), consisting of supreme mantra-syllables, is named Trailokyavijaya.

It is remembered as consisting of all castes, yet it is not to be revealed, not to be given, not to be heard, and not to be spoken by a wicked person, one of low birth, or one who has not been initiated.
"It must not be given to one who has fallen away;
'it must not be given'—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
It should not be given to one who is uninitiated, nor to one devoid of austerity and the like."
By reciting this armor-mantra (*kavaca*), the practitioner who possesses power and devotion becomes initiated;
this armor of the Lord is supreme, consisting of perfected knowledge, and must be kept secret.
This secret, consisting of the knowledge of Brahman,
which bestows desired fruits upon its devotees and is the sovereign for victory over the three worlds, has not been told to anyone; remember it!
By merely bowing, the goddess becomes instantly submissive;
by reciting and wearing this armor (*kavaca*) of the Lord, the heroic practitioner wanders fearlessly in the Kali age.
When a practitioner of mantras, desiring to fight, enters into battle while recollecting this armor-mantra of Thāhlīṃ-Bagalāmukhī,
he should recite the Lord of Armor three times for his protection.
Having conquered his enemies who are like Time itself,
the practitioner, having placed upon his head the armor containing the mantra, shall return to his own home.
O Maheśvarī, by placing the *tuka* armor upon the throat of the practitioner, he can suddenly bring all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, under his control;
they come into his subjection.
The host of Apsarases, beginning with Hasārambhā,
[protects] during terrible portents, various fears,
and diseases; this armor contains the essence of mantras.
The person who recites this armor (kavaca) of the goddess Śrī-Devī Avalokiteśvarī, which is very difficult to obtain, shall find peace from whatever fear arises through action, mind, or speech.
This [teaching] named Trailokyavijaya should not be given to anyone who is of low birth, who is deluded,
who is devoid of devotion, who is hypocritical, or who is possessed by greed.
O Lord, this armor-mantra (*kavaca*) must never be given to a disciple,
even if he is endowed with devotion and dedicated to his guru,
provided he is free from greed and hypocrisy.
Let it be given even to those who are not devotees; by giving to his sons, a man may become afflicted with leprosy. At night, the giver should perform a bath, worship, and go home with a lamp.
O Maheśānī, having recited this supreme armor-mantra with the root of the *jjvālya* [mantra],
even if it be the dead of night,
the lord of the realm will come to one's house.
O Goddess, daughter of the mountain, this truth of the gods has been told by me without doubt; it is a peaceful armor, O Goddess, to be guarded, more to be guarded, and as secret as one's own womb.
Thus ends the *Bhagalāmukhī Mantra Astra-Kavaca*, as spoken in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Tantra* within the dialogue between Maheśvara; may it be auspicious.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Bagalāmukhī. Oṃ,
on the delightful peak of the Himālaya mountain, cool, endowed with jewels,
filled with various trees, and meritorious like the Gaṅgā...

To the Lord of the Gods, the Blessed One, the Teacher of the World, the compassionate Supreme Sovereign, who was seated comfortably with Pārvatī and accompanied by hosts of Gaṇas and Gandharvas singing—
I meditate upon the Supreme Lord worshipped by Rāvaṇa, the tranquil Master who bestows boons and fearlessness, who wears a mass of matted hair, the Lord of the three worlds,
smiling and adorned with ashes.
Seeing that Raṃ was pleased, Gaurī, the mother of the world, spoke to Giriśa. The Goddess said: "O Śaṅkara, whose crest is adorned by the crescent moon, who are worshipped by gods and demons!"
"O Destroyer of Tripura, O God of gods, O Great Lord, you previously granted me a boon; it behoves you to grant that to me now.
Īśvara said: "By me, [the truth has been spoken]..."
"O you of excellent vows, choose a boon granted by me. The Goddess said:
"O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, O Bhava, O Śambhu, [grant me] the Thousand Names of the Goddess Śrī Vagalāmukhī."

The Thousand Names of Mantra. The Lord said: This secret, which fulfills all desires, has been told to you alone; it must be guarded with great effort, even as one would protect a fraction of a digit.
It bestows repetition (*vīpsita*), as well as subjugation (*vaśīkāra*), attraction (*kṛṣṭi*), hatred (*vidveṣa*), paralysis (*staṃbhana*), delusion (*mohana*),
and even killing (*māraṇa*); it is always to be worshipped by practitioners (*sādhaka*s).
O Goddess, whatever evil deeds have been committed by men throughout hundreds of millions of *kalpas*,
that sin shall reach pacification merely by the recollection of this secret.
O best of beings who accomplish what is difficult to achieve, this question is not to be spoken; this boon is not to be granted.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, O Śarva, choose a boon!
The beloved Śrī Devī said: "O Lord of Gods, you shall proclaim the thousand names of the mantra of the goddess Śrī Vagalāmukhī; there is no delay."

"Do not worry," said the illustrious Lord. "Listen, O Goddess, for out of devotion to you I shall proclaim that which grants all desires in the Kali age; it must be kept strictly secret from the wicked and even from those who harbor hatred."
Of this Thousand-Name Hymn of Śrī Vagalāmukhī, the Seer is Śrī Bhairava, the Meter is Anuṣṭubh,
and the Deity is the Goddess Śrī Vagalāmukhī.
*Hlīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hlāṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *svāhā* is the pin (*kīlaka*);
this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the recitation of the *Thousand Names of Vagalamukhī* for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
Then, for the meditation: [one should visualize her] yellow in color, wearing yellow matted locks, destroying enemies, joyful, with a smiling face,
and with her crest adorned by a digit of the moon and fire-moons.

One should meditate upon the supreme Goddess Śrī Bagalāmukhī, whose form is compassion, who has eyes like the sun, who is dark-complexioned, adorned with bright yellow garlands, and possesses uplifted, straight breasts.
Having meditated thus, the practitioner of mantra should remember [the deity] after performing the ritual of *nyāsa*:
*oṃ hlīṃ bagalāmukhi sarvaduṣṭavācaṃ padaṃ staṃbhaya staṃbhaya jī*.
Hvāṃ kīlaya kīlaya buddhiṃ vināśaya vināśaya hrīṃ oṃ svāhā. Now the nyāsa:
oṃ hlāṃ aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ; oṃ hlīṃ tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ.

Oṃ nīṃ, salutation to the two index fingers; Oṃ hlūṃ, salutation to the two middle fingers; Oṃ hlaiṃ, salutation to the two ring fingers; Oṃ hlauṃ, salutation to the two little fingers; Oṃ hlaḥ, salutation to the palms of the hands.
"Oṃ, salutation to the backs of the hands"—thus is the *karanyāsa*.
Now follows the *ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*: "Oṃ hlāṃ, salutation to the heart;
Oṃ hlīṃ, svāhā to the head; hluṃ to the crest (*śikhā*)."
Vaṣaṭ! Oṃ hlaiṃ, huṃ to the armor; oṃ hroṃ, vaṣaṭ to the three eyes; oṃ hlaḥ, phaṭ to the weapon. Thus, one should perform the ritual of placement (nyāsa).
One should recite this thousand names,
which is not to be disclosed, supremely secret, and bestows what is desired in the Kali age: *Oṃ hlīṃ vālāvali jñeyā*.
She who bestows both validity and invalidity, who moves within the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), who is Brahmic, purified by Brahman, worshipped by the gods, the Mistress of Brahmā,
the Daughter of Brahmā, and the very embodiment of Brahman itself.
She is the embodied one, consisting of the light of Brahman,
worshipped by Nanda and Sunda; she is the Mistress of Bliss, established in the Nandana grove, and is Śivā, eternally composed of bliss.
Clad in worn-out garments, with thick and full breasts,
she was the auspicious path for both merit and demerit; she was the meritorious woman who leads others to the next world, the ancient one, higher than the highest.

The army of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva), which possesses the form of the Ancient Puruṣa, is honored by the city-dwellers; it is served by the city of Tripura and bestows victory upon the Foe of Tripura (Śiva).
May that army, which is dear to Padmā (Lakṣmī) who holds a lotus, be pleased with me.
The mistress of that city, the daughter of Siddha,
Paulomī, the daughter of Puloman, radiant, drinking [the nectar], with full limbs and thick arms.
She who is dear to him, who is startled by grey hair,
whose lute-strings are broken, who is like a female monkey, who possesses matted locks, and who is the wife of the one who has attained the wealth of the bamboo flute.
The protector of discernment, the jewel among women, the mother of heroes, the fertile ground, the sovereign lady, the soul of the universe, the creator of the universe—
she is Kālī, whose form is Time itself, the stainless one.
She possesses a luster like that of a smokeless,
smoky-grey Śivā; she is the sovereign lady of the gods, with limbs distinguished by great splendor, a playful woman of the common folk, tawny-hued, and with reddish-brown hair.
The daughter of Gu, the sister of Yama,
the daughter of Yamī, endowed with glory, possessing splendor, her face resembling the moon, Śānti, joined with peace, Antikā, Śarvāṇī, and she whose body is Śiva.

Sthāśiveśvarī, the bestower of auspiciousness and the performer of both good and evil deeds, she who possesses anklets and a girdle of stars, the pure one, the object of meditation, the one of soft limbs, and she who is worshipped by the Lord of Māṇḍavī.

She who is honored by the unmanifest, who is the limit of the mind, who is free from impurity, who holds a skull-bowl in her hand, who is intoxicated by the honey-wine, and who is reeling from the essence of that honey-wine—she is Mādhvī. In former times, she was the earth, the Malatī vine, the intellect,
the spring breeze, the intoxicated moonlight, the night, the goddess of fortune, the sky, the path, and joy.
She who resembles a lotus with golden petals, whose birth is a web of splendor,
who removes the dullness of the earth’s light, who is beloved by the world,
who is both the eldest and the youngest, who is purchased [by love], and whose limbs are tender.
Kalaṅkinī, Kālī, Kālapriyā, Kulyā, Krodhinī, Kāñcanaprabhā, Kāmyā, Kārāgṛhasthā, and Kāmanākausaleśvarī.
Goddess Śīdā, who bestows fame, brings security, is composed, patient, fond of forbearance, free from hunger, devoid of the thirst for worldly existence,
and provides washed garments.
She was a maiden of the Vaka clan,
a daughter of the Naga race, a young woman of the serpent lineage; she was modest, with limbs bent low in humility,
wearing fresh garments and a brand-new girdle.
The Nīti-nīti (the practice of policy) was filled with the sound of anklets;
she possessed the luster of a lotus and a lotus-stalk,
and she was a boat for navigators, a bow, and a steel arrow.

She who possesses a form of knots, who delights in religious observances, whose speech is like that of a leaf-eater, who is devoted to song, whose splendor is radiant, who is pleased by power, and who rejoices in the sovereignty of the city.
She who sports in the Nandana grove, she who is accessible through the play of the Discus, she who is dear to the virtuous, she who wields the mace, she who removes disease,
she who possesses the speed of the marrow-wind— may she, the giver of pride, protect me.
She who bestows memory and takes away memory, she who is memory itself and the agent of mental impressions, she who is forgetfulness,
free from pride, humble, victorious, and pure knowledge.
Bathed in the radiance of Vairocana, with full-limbed form,
the witness of all beings,
impassioned yet ever-devoted, the beloved protector of Gajanana, she who is seated upon the lord of elephants.
She is the mistress of the Gaṇas, worshipped by the Gaṇas and Gandharvas;
she is the path of the Gandharvīs and Kinnarīs, accessible through sacred hymns, the form that is to be attained, the goddess Gāruḍī, and she who is honored by Garuḍa.
The form of Maheśvara is she who laughs aloud, who is rich in honey, the elephant-like one,
worshipped by sages, the mistress of men, intoxicated with pride,
and devoted to the drinking of honey.
Vaṭeśvarī, whose eyes are reddened by the wine of passion,
who holds a lute in her hand like the goddess Vāruṇī,
and who is clothed in garments as red as the twilight.
O Mother, you who shake off the forest fire with your snare, who hold a weapon in your hand, whose hands are the tongues of enemies, who crush your foes,
and who paralyze with a mallet in your hand— [I bow to you].
She who is honored by the great ministers and lords of the Maghas, Malāvatī, Mahāmānī, and Indrāṇī; she who is Ramā,
Revā, Raviṃdākṣī, and Raviṃduśikhilocanā.
She who is the beloved of Revatī, whose lover was consumed by Rāma’s amorous passion; she who is Rohiṇī of lovely form,
adorned with ornaments of jewels, and a mine of gems.
She who delights in the undertaking of what is dear, who is served by those who find joy in her,
who is the sovereign lady of Rāma, whose fortune is pure,
who possesses golden anklets, and who is beloved by Rukmāṅgada in the ocean.
Rama, whose form is that of the lover; the garland of flavors consisting of the six tastes; adorned with two tongues;
fearless; the remover of fear; the destroyer of delusion; the formidable one; dear to Bharga.
The city of Māhiṣmatī was like the twilight of truth, possessing a foundation of truthful resolve; its people were cheerful, eager, serene,
modest, and possessed of hanging tresses of hair.
She who brings joy to the pot-bellied one (Gaṇeśa), who destroys the suffering of women, who delights in the sound of "Klīm," who consumes the grain of modesty,
and who is the creeper-like vine of the Vetāla.
She who assumes the guise of a courtesan from Lāṭā, who supports the forest, who acts for the forest, who is the presiding deity of the trees,
who is beloved by those who roam the woods, and who is the essence of the Vedas.
She is beloved by Śiva, a speaker of truth, the source of speech,
the mother of heroes, the subduer of the brave,
the bestower of boons, the most excellent one, and the companion of Viṣṇu.
The beloved woman, who speaks like a noble lady, who brings about the destruction of leprosy and other diseases, who is of evil course yet possesses a beautiful gait,
who is Kuntī, the crusher of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas.
She is the splendor of the Kauravas and Pāṇḍavas, the bestower of splendor, the embodiment of beauty, accessible to the lions of Kāśī,
beloved by saffron, possessing a tuft of hair, and hailing from Kaśmīra.
I bow to her who dwells in the lotus-abode of the beloved of Ruru,
who is the vine of compassion for Mādhava, who is embraced by Mādhava, and who is the city of Amarāvatī, Mathurā, and Ujjayinī.
Yogyā, Ayodhyā, Kṣayaṃkarī, Yajñeśī, Jñābhuktā, Vyāghrā, Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Ghasadā, Yaśovatī, Cārvaṅgī, and Candrabhāgā.
The night, whose flickering tongue is the moonlight,
who sports with the mountain-like Cāru (the moon), who wears the mountain as her crest-ornament, and who removes the fire of separation, is the mother to be known.
The Vitastā, beloved by Vasudeva, the abode of the giver of wealth,
worshipped by the Vārccitas, possessing the form of the Paulomī river, arising from the Pāravāra mountain, complete in all her parts.
The virtuous Sarayū, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, Mandākinī, Satyā, Sādhupūjyā, Sureśvarī, and Yamunā— all desirous of battle.
She is served by yoginīs, she who is mounted upon a horse, who dwells upon an elephant, and who rides Airāvata;
she is like the Airāvatī, the Vetravatī, and the Nārasiṃhī rivers.
She who is the mistress of the treasury of the gods, the lotus-eyed one,
beloved by the gods, the bull among asuras,
she who reclines upon the ocean, and is worshipped by the one who sleeps upon the sea.
She who is the form of the bridge, the sovereign of all, always possessing every form; she who is the restless one with a restless gait,
the playful one, the dweller in the kūrca grass, the mistress of the reeds, and the sovereign of the reeds.

The salutation to those who are to be censured, those worthy of worship, and those who are neither— this is one's own; the sweat on the face, the essential and the non-essential, the essence from the non-essence, the three confluences, the three paths, and the triple age (tretā)— [all these constitute the path].
She who is worshipped by Tryakṣī and Tryambaka; Tārā, Cogro, Prabhā, Ghorā, Cogratārā, Catāriṇī,
Ugreśvarī, Cograbuddhi, and Ugrarūpā.
She who possesses the three Vedas, who is modest, who destroyed the three cities,
who is the destroyer of the Asuras of the three cities, who is the consort of the enemy of Tripura, who is the support of the three worlds, who is the savior, and who assumes the form of the dawn.
She who is beloved by each and every youth, who takes the form of the three fires, who is the triple Veda, the mistress of the mountain king (Śiva),
and the terrifier of gods and demons— may she grant me prosperity.
She is the lineage of the hand, the sovereign of the ocean,
the slayer of the demon Śumbha, the remover of Niśumbha’s pride,
the three-fold twilight, and the aging at the junctions of time.
The constant movement of the wind-god, always moving,
who is practiced by those who move, worshipped by the immortals,
the night-walker who removes disease, the protector of those who roam at night.
Yaṅkarī, Rāvaṇeṣṭā, Carantī, Iṣṭā, Rākṣasī, Ghorālocanā, Koṭarākṣī,
Padmākṣī, Mṛgākṣī, and Komalālakā.
She is served by the lord of beasts, she is immortal, she possesses mantras, she is dear to mantra-practitioners, she is the grandmother, she is the destroyer of death,
she is supreme as the mother of the fathers and grandfathers, and she is clad in yellow garments.
Adorned with garlands and ornaments dear to her yellow hue, possessing full breasts, she is the hope for the love of the pigeon-colored one; Śacī,
the beloved of Indra, and likewise Rudrāṇī.
Śarvāṇī, honored by Śarva; Vaiṣṇavī, worshipped by Viṣṇu; Kaumārī, whose seat is fire;
Kauverī, the mistress of the Yakṣas, clad in silken garments.
She is the sacrificial rite that bestows glory, copper-hued, consisting of song, having the form of the three atoms, Urvaśī,
with eyes like raw meat, and the slayer of the flesh-eaters.
She is the creator of the universe, the sovereign of all, worshipped by Viśvaṃbhara; she is the sustainer of the world,
the earth, the supporter, the wish-fulfilling cow, the source of nourishment, and the beloved of Brahmā.
Stability, brilliance, swift and rapid movement, compassion,
invincibility from the fortress situated in the eight corners,
the light of one difficult to conquer, and a radiance like a thousand suns and moons.
I worship the Goddess who possesses the three forms and the three jewels, who is like a sapphire, white, the mistress of Chinnamastā, the sovereign, the bearer of the parasol,
fond of the parasol, and the one to be meditated upon.
She who is the stride of Yama, the pride of the arrogant slave-girl, the embodiment of the lunar days, the guileless one; she who causes terror through her own fearlessness,
the sharp one, and she whose form is the brilliance of fierce flames.

Possessing the incomparable luster of a circle [of light] from her forehead and hand, and possessing incomparable valor; she who is worthy of praise, whose nature consists of praise, who is blissful, who bestows happiness, who has a beautiful face, and whose fame is like the moon.
She whose crest is both unpeaceful and peaceful in form, the Sovereign of Śiva, who is auspicious yet possesses a non-terrible roar, whose nature is both sleep and wakefulness,
the Mistress of Gold, and whose shanks are [beautiful].
[I bow] to Rikā, Śāradā, Śivā, Bhavānī, Bhadrakālī, Mahiṣāsurasūdinī,
Mahiṣasthā, Mahiṣī, and Mūlādhārā.
Lāpahā, Śrī, Śobhā, she who holds a lotus in her hand, the destroyer of the destruction of the Lotus-born (Brahmā), Padmā, beloved of the lotus-eyed one, worshipped by Mahākāla.
Śmaśānavāsinī, Kālī, Kulikā, Cārakaulinī, Kāmavatī, Kāmaga,
Kāmalolā, Kalānidhi, and Kalā.
Her crest is adorned with a garland of skulls;
she is the playful moonlight for the night-lotus of her devotees;
she is worshipped by Kūrta; she is the embodiment of the power of Kātyāyanī.
She who removes the stains of impurity when embraced, who is desired by those free from disease, who possesses the endurance of a great archer,
and who is richly adorned with golden ornaments on her arms.
She who wears golden armlets,
who is the daughter of Pulaha and the wife of Pulaka, who is the slayer of the son of Pulastya,
and who increases the lineage of grandsons and great-grandsons.
She is the foot-soldier, the wife, the cloud, the fang, the drinker, the beloved, she whose ornaments are drunk, she with the tawny face, she with the tawny hair,
she with the tawny garments, she who possesses water, the meritorious, and the non-meritorious.
She is the destination for those dwelling in the worlds of merit and demerit;
she is the Queen served by the lords of kings, the Sovereign of the Kings of Kings, the Radiant One,
the one whose soul is merit, and the bestower of merit.
She who increases merit, desired merit, and demerit; O Lord of Night, she whose face is auspicious; she who is white and the sovereign of the meritorious;
the mistress of Tripura, the city of cities, and the full sovereign of cities.

She who possesses various forms, whose appearance is as formidable as Bhairava, who is radiant with light, worshipped by Bhārgava, the sovereign of the Bhārgavas, the daughter of Bhṛgu, and the bestower of poetic genius upon the sons of Bhṛgu.
She who is served by the Vidyādharas, she who dwells on the Vindhya mountains, the sovereign of poets and living beings, the victorious one,
the increaser of victory, and she who belongs to Kosala.
Kausalyā, Akupyā, Akupitamānasā, Kopinī, Kurukulyā,
Cakamanīyā, Cakaṅkaṇī, Kulajā, Āḍākinī, and Dāntā.
She is the destroyer of darkness, the remover of delusion;
she is the sovereign of the pit of the Rajas-quality, the assembly of the Tamas-quality, and the one who delights in the teeth, the giver of the end of pride, and the one who is beyond all deceit.
Free from worldly existence, she is by nature like a dancer; she is skilled in dancing, singing, and instrumental music, and she brings delight to Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and their consorts.
She who is the Yoga-sleep of Nārāyaṇa, worshipped by yogis, the abode of the ages, the creator of the ages, and the sovereign of the ages;
she who is the Yoginī, moving through the sky, flying through the air, and wielding a celestial chariot.
With eyes like those of a peacock, a hand resting on her hip, and a frown upon her brow;
fair-complexioned yet possessing a formidable form, with a face like a crow’s and a crest like a peak;
she who devours the Palāśa tree, who dwells among herds of cows, and whose speech is like the sound of a drum.
She who is the essence of Bharata, beloved of Bharata; the sister of Govinda on the banks of the Godāvarī; she whose gait is like that of a bird;
she who is tranquil; she who holds a khaṭvāṅga staff in her hand; she who possesses the brilliance of ten million suns.
She is equal to all, captivating, holding a mace in her hand,
worshipped by Hāṭakeśvara, having removed the greed of Hastinī, immovable, and possessing an unattainable form.
She whose path is the tears from her own eyes, who possesses the sound of the cricket (*cīrī*),

who is the army of the earth, who wears a garment of skin, who is beloved by the nectar of immortality, whose limbs are like sandalwood, from whom the tresses have fallen, and who is the cleverness of the four [Vedas].
She who reclines upon the four oceans of blood,
who is beloved by the four Vedas, who is self-controlled, who bestows the fruits of the four ages, and who yields the equal fruit of the four aims of human life.
Adorned with the seed-syllable (bīja), situated within two or four corners,
resting in the place of the drop (bindu),
having the form of the Drop (vaidavī), and being the auspicious Sāvitrī, she is indeed the Vaidhavī.
The sovereign goddess, residing in a thousand abodes,
is the ascetic woman who is the fruit of austerities; she is established in penance, honored by those whose wealth is austerity through their practice of asceticism.
She who is the crossing over the mass of darkness, whose own form is like molten copper, who is established in the jar, who is not terrible despite her formidable nature,
whose army consists of fierce-eyed women, and who is the female monkey.

I am the destroyer of tomorrow, the creator of all, the sovereign of the universe, born of a noble lineage, born of the family of Akula, the female swan, possessing the gait of a swan, the chin, the nourisher of Hara,
the daughter of Hari, and the lioness.
She who takes away the wife, who is the sovereign mistress, whose hand holds the weapon, who is the oblation, worship, the act of worshipping, and the form of the boat;
she whose eyes are the oblation, who is the end of the syllable "Haṃ," and who is the beautiful form of the principle of ego (ahaṃkṛti).
She is richly adorned with ornaments beginning with the letter *ṇa*, her head adorned with a crescent moon; she is the beloved of those who bow before her,
the destroyer of the life of enemies, and the bestower of life, the Mistress of the Krama.
Kramyā, whose nature is Akūrā, is worshipped as the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī);
she is Kroḍinī, whose form is within Klāṃ, the pure-minded one ending with Kroḍīśa; Cāmuṇḍī, Muṇḍa...
She who cuts off Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa from her hand, the fierce Caṇḍikā,
of fierce form and fierce laughter, the source of wonder;
she who bestows auspiciousness, residing upon the chest of Śiva.
She is worshipped by Viṣṇu, she holds a knife and a sword in her hands, she possesses an umbrella, she is the cutter,
she is of the nature of a fissure, she has a piercing intellect, and she is the deceiver.
She wanders at night, appearing like a Cāṇḍālī woman with the form of leftovers;
she moves with the gait of an elephant in rut, and she traverses the peaks of Trikūṭa, the mountain bestowed by Kubera.
She who dwells in ten million noble families, she who is born of noble lineage, she who possesses a multitude of noble qualities;
she who is dark-complexioned, she whose face is dark, she who destroys pride, she who is the mistress of women, she whose form is dark, she who [removes] cold and heat.
She is the radiance of the beloved, blazing with a complexion of light;
she is the flame of the letters beginning with *ka*, ending with *kṣa*; she is the fourfold self, the four states of existence, the lover of dance, and the female dancer.
Dhūrtā, Dhūrtavarapradā, Dhūmrārcis, Dhūmravastrā, Dhūmrā, Dhūmranibhā,
as well as Vārāhī, Dhūmraśabdā, and Kālarātri.
She is beloved by the world, the embodiment of the syllable Om,
Kujā, Vāṇī, Sarasvatī, the vernacular tongue, the Mleccha tongue, refined culture, and the lack of refinement.
And Jananī Jānakī herself is free from old age and death;
though aged, she is essentially young; though satisfied, she is insatiable, with a mind that transcends the mundane; she is the creation and the sustenance.
The goddess Karī, likewise the bringer of dissolution,
the one who effects expulsion and subjugation, the woman who wanders in the forest,
and she whose tongue is made mute by the left.
Dwelling in the forest of virtuous conduct, she was a banner of dharma and adharma; firm in body yet firm in her senses,
she had conquered her senses and subdued her anger— sweet, yet not like honey.
Rākṣasā, Madhurī, Madhurālāpā, Vālā,
Vālavalipriyā, Jvālāsmā,
Śikhājvālā, Jāntā, and likewise Jvālāmukhī.
Aghahartrī, Sarvajñā, Jñānarūpā, Laṃpilā, Padmāvatī, Vratacarā, Preman,
Pativratā, Indirā, and Candrā.

She who dwells in the center of the solar orb situated between the two poles, Dakṣā, Dākṣāyaṇī, and she who destroyed the sacrifice of Dakṣa; Śiśumātr̥ (Mother of the Child) and Śiśūtsaṅgā (Embracing the Child).
She who removes the pride of Śiśupāla, who is clad in dark garments, who dwells upon the body of Śiva, who takes the form of a hunter, and who is the sovereign of the arrow;
she is both pleased and wrathful, yet she is the satisfaction that is beyond all comparison here.

She who is fond of the *pulīta*, *tālīya*, *tālu*, *kātu*, *lyā*, *tulasī*, and *mālatī* flowers; she who possesses the splendor of a swarm of bees; she who removes the delusion of worldly existence; she who is the Sovereign of Delusion (*Bhrameśvarī*).
Reaching to the clouds, situated amidst the clouds, and wandering as far as the netherworld and the surface of the earth;
she who eats the fruit of the jackfruit tree,
stands in the midst of a row, possesses offspring, and has a tender body.
O Camuṣatā, wielder of the mace-weapon,
you who take away the enchanting garland of mantras consisting of the syllable *anu*,
O Vali, you whose form is the heart, O Kāmeśā, [salutations] a hundred times!

She who is served through ritual, who brings auspiciousness to Śaṅkara, who is desired, who bestows the auspicious, whose form is auspicious, who is the pinnacle of the auspicious lineage, and who is the pride of the proud women.
She who bestows the river, whose song is the vulva, whose song is the phallus,
who rests upon the vulva and the phallus, who is fond of the vulva, whose abode is the vulva, the ground of existence, and she who is worshipped by kings.
She who wears a garland of *vakula* flowers vomited [by the gods], she whose beloved is the *atilaka*, she who is a garland of *aśoka* trees yet is herself free from sorrow (*aśoka*),
she who removes grief and brings about auspiciousness, and she who swiftly bestows prosperity.
Bharūpā, Bhadradā, Bhadrakālikā, Siddhā, Siddhapriyā, Sādhyā, Siddhidā,

She who is honored by the Sāṃvatas, she who is the source of the Sāman-chants, she who is peaceful, she who delights in the singing of the Sāmans, she who grants prosperity,
she who is beloved by the Ṛbhus, she who is the Ṛbhu, and she whose color is that of the Ṛks.

Adorned with ornaments, she possesses a form that is both austere and beautiful; she moves upon the surface of the earth like a female ascetic, and her body is illuminated by the splendor of penance performed for the sake of removing the threefold suffering.

She who accomplishes the means of accomplishment, she who is the accomplisher of the accomplisher, she who is without a brother, she who is the practice of accomplishment, she who is tireless, she who is well-being,
she whose splendor is Sthāṇu, she whose form is Sthāṇu, she who is dear to the wielder of the trident.
She who destroys the disease of colic with her hand that holds a trident, who bestows a firm and robust physical form, whose very essence is the stability of the bones,
and who is as massive as the *svayambhū* flower.
She is the self-existent one, she who moves through heaven, she whose gait is heaven, she who is the firmament, she who is the sky, the mistress of the lords of the jewels of liberation,
the lake of the navel, the ocean, and the lunar day.
Worshipped by the wise, she removes physical pain and mental anguish;
she is the destroyer of heat and the remover of suffering; she wears a girdle of skulls, dwells upon corpses, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads and eyes.
She who is the sovereign of men, worshipped by men, honored by Indra (Naravāhana), whose name is Nāma, whose form is humility,
whose body is cool, who moves with coolness, and who bestows well-being upon the Lord.

O Śrī Devī Avagalāmukhī, this thousand-name hymn has been recounted by me to you out of devotion;
it must never be disclosed. [It is effective] in paralyzing and in slaying.
O Goddess, do not forget [this] in times of terrible enemy conflict, great fear, fear of kings, or fear born of thieves and fire,
nor in fear of great portents.
This *Nāmasāhasraka* brings about that supreme tranquility,
just as water does in the heat of summer;
it is the bestower of boons, the remover of worldly existence, and the secret of all purposes.
By the mere remembrance of this,
all sin is destroyed; this thousand names bestows the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O beloved, whatever fruit is obtained from bathing in sacred fords such as Puṣkara, a living being attains that same fruit by remembering the Thousand Names; this is a secret.
This [place] is delightful, bestowing the fruit of ten million sacrifices,
meritorious, a granter of merit, pure, and increasing one's sons and grandsons; it should be remembered for the sake of pacifying great calamities.
If a mortal, having risen at dawn, should recite, cause to be recited, or hear this *Rennāmasahasrakam*,
that [attainment] shall be within the grasp of that mortal.
Having risen at dawn,
one should write this mantra-empowered yantra, which grants all accomplishments, upon birch bark or a tooth-stick using ink made from *kukuma*, *kastūrī*, sandalwood, and other substances.
One should write the Thousand Names of the illustrious goddess Avalāmukhī; outside of that, there should be an eight-pointed figure, a triangle,
and a four-petalled lotus, followed by three circles.
Then, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus;
thereafter, having drawn three concentric circles provided with four gates, [one should place] the Mistress of the Yantra, Vagalāmukhī.
The knower of mantras, being ever heroic, should write [the mantra] upon birch bark; he should then wrap it with yellow cloth. Thereafter, O Great Goddess, one should place gold upon that yantra.
Having placed the Lord of the Yantra upon his head,
the practitioner who masters the mantra shall wander through the three worlds as a hero, just like the Unstruck One (Ahaṃ).
Holding this in his left hand, the master of mantras should paralyze the enemy by force;
always wearing this yantra on his neck,
he may engage in enjoyment with a woman through action or thought.
O Lord of the Yantra, if a woman who has many sons becomes menstruating while wearing [the yantra],
she will become barren when the tenth month arrives on the fifth day.
O Maheśānī, by holding this yantra in one's heart and reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times, one shall obtain a son and bring the three worlds under one's control.

In the Kali age, the prescribed method for the preliminary rite (purascarya) of the Śrī Devīs, headed by Vagalāmukhī, is as follows: whoever performs it one hundred times over shall become equal to Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices.

A person should recite it once for the sake of attaining the fruit of ten million sacrifices; a wise person should perform it ten times for the sake of obtaining a vision of the Goddess. Valī and samatā [are the two types of recitation].
The practitioner possesses a power of breath equal to the wind;
he is like me in knowledge, O Goddess, resembling the intellect of Brahmā,
and like Śukra in poetic skill.
Resplendent like fire through his valor and resembling the sun in brilliance,
he shall become the minister of this [king] by virtue of reciting [this].
Merely by the recitation of these thousand names—
O Maheśvarī, for which practitioner will Vagalāmukhī become a beloved daughter? What need is there to say more here regarding the power of the practitioner?
The deity who instructs the son of Kobagalā—
having enjoyed happiness in this world,
one shall attain liberation after death; this is the supreme secret.
O Goddess of the Suras, I have declared this most secret, supreme secret, the very essence of all things, known as the *Vagalāmukhī*.
It must not be given to anyone whatsoever; it must not be given, O Maheśvarī.

The lord of the earth becomes scorched; Vaiśvānara (fire) becomes cold;

salutations to you! (4) Indeed, these mantras are sufficient to overcome adversaries.
O Mother Śrī Vagalāmukhī, you are the pure *daḷane-stotra*, the *yantra* that restrains all, the conqueror of the three worlds, and the armor (*tatra*) [of protection]. Your name is most beautiful.
Because of the utterance of your name by that living being in the assembly, his mouth shall become paralyzed,
and his wicked speech shall be violently suppressed.
May it be for my sight a destroyer of sins, a pacifier of afflictions, a dispeller of poverty, a subduer of kings, a magnet that attracts the hearts of fawn-eyed women,

Pierce the tip of his tongue with the Brahmī-mudrā, awaken his intellect, paralyze the movement of his sun-like eyes,
